<reason>CON identified early and maintained throughout that the motion covers somatic, self-regarding recreational enhancement by consenting adults, while most of PRO's harm stories (embryos, germline, grandchildren) target a category PRO himself admits is already banned elsewhere. This scope pressure was never fully resolved by PRO. PRO's best counter—an "enforcement collapse" argument claiming the somatic/germline line is unverifiable so the whole category must be banned—was clever but ran straight into CON's "proves too much" reductio: the same unverifiability applies to therapeutic somatic gene therapy, which PRO never wants banned and never addressed in rebuttal or closing. CON's closing crystallized this unanswered gap cleanly, while PRO's closing repeated the enforcement-collapse point without patching the hole. CON's cosmetic-surgery/braces/hormones analogies and licensing-vs-ban framing were consistently deployed and never fully neutralized, giving CON the cleaner, more resolved path to victory despite both sides suffering a clipped turn.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's "proves too much" point in Rebuttal 2/Closing (B4.2, B5.3-B5.4)—that PRO's unverifiability argument for banning recreational somatic edits would equally justify banning somatic gene therapy for disease—landed and was never answered by PRO in the final speech.</best_rebuttal>
